Abeka sells Protestant Christian homeschooling materials. I used their Pre-K and Kindergarten Math books with my kids when they were that age. You can search by grade level and just pick which books you'd like to use.

Seton is a Catholic homeschool publisher. I've used their workbooks in the past: spelling, handwriting, religion, English. I order my testing materials through them. They also have great books for parents on homeschooling and parenting in general--I highly recommend "Character Building".

I use lots of Classical Academic Press materials. I see that they do have a Preschool curriculum, which looks great.

I recommend the books "Designing Your Own Classical Curriculum" by Berquist and "Well Trained Mind" by Susan Bauer. I also recommend looking into Charlotte Mason homeschooling.

Suggestions for preschool:

Get a Pre-K Math curriculum. It'll be the basics of writing numbers and counting and stuff, but good to do every day for about a half hour or so. "Counting bears" or geometric shapes manipulatives are fun at that age.

Read aloud chapter books every day. Get the kid to read at his or her level for at least a half hour every day.

Copywork (lines from poems or Bible verses) for handwriting and spelling. Have the kid illustrate the words with a drawing. Can take a half hour or a little longer, depending on the intensity of the artwork.

Child-sized masterpieces for art. PreK art curriculum like Artistic Pursuits. Kids love art. This could take like a half hour to an hour.

Informal history. Reading books borrowed from the library that feature various time periods around the world. A Day on Skates comes to mind as an example of Netherlands history in the early 1900s.

Informal science. Nature studies: go outside and observe nature in a pond, river, or woods. There is a book "Mudpies To Magnets" that I remember being good for the preschool ages. Watch nature documentaries (kids just love David Attenborough documentaries).

Cook together. Play logic board games together. Get into crafty skills together. And try to do a "1 hour quiet time" after lunch or so, where everyone is in their own room or own space and can read, play, nap, or relax on their own. Have fun!

Both my reading children read way above their age level, and my 4.5 year old is just beginning to show interest in reading, and he's going to find it a lot easier because he already knows the sounds most of the phonograms make when reading.

Depending on what kind of preschool you had your kiddo in, you're probably better off homeschooling anyways. Preschools are inundated with students with disabilities...which wouldn't be so bad except that many many many of them have severe and/or aggressive behaviors. I would focus on fine motor skills, days of the week, counting, basic place value, months, seasons, name writing when ready, dolch or fry sight words if your kid is ready, sorting, and letter tracing. A-z reading is a resource you have to pay for...but at age 3 to 4 could be a great resource to start teaching reading. The online books and lessons are printable.

We homeschool our children, and really like the Saxon Math program (As long as you buy the books that are 1st or 2nd edition. After that, the Saxon family sold the company, and it was inundated with Common Core material, making it inferior.). It's play-based, but covers everything a preschool child would need to know. They will also put your child ahead, actually. My 5 year old really likes it, and I'm starting my 4 year old in it as well. It would require you to buy a manipulatives set. We also use Spell to Write and Read, but if you're just doing it casually, I'm not sure if it is something you want to get into. It's a fantastic program that teaches phonetically, and teaches the rules of the English language in such a way that there aren't many exceptions, and it's logical. There are also great free online supports if you have any questions. I pair it with their Cursive First program.

We joined a homeschooling co-op called Classical Conversations. They are a Christ-centered co-op, and we signed a statement of faith before we joined up. It can get pricey, but if you become a tutor, the pay will pretty much pay for your kids tuition (and then some, depending on how many kids you have). If there isn't one in your area, you could look into becoming a Director and start your own. :) They meet once a week for 24 weeks out of the year. It goes all the way through high school, and provides the education my husband and I WISH we would've received.
